questions.stem: During a colonoscopy, the patient opens her eyes and says "okay" only after you firmly squeeze her trapezius twice. Which depth of sedation is she in?
options: Deep sedation
Moderate sedation
General anesthesia
Minimal sedation
questions.explanation: Purposeful response only after repeated or painful stimulation defines deep sedation. Moderate sedation responds to voice or light touch; general anesthesia is unarousable even to pain.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: During a propofol infusion for an ERCP, the patient does not open his eyes to his name or a shoulder shake. A firm trapezius squeeze makes him pull his arm toward his chest and grimace, then he goes still. His respiratory rate is 8 with a jaw thrust. What is his depth, and what does the withdrawal tell you?
options: At least deep sedation; reflex withdrawal is not a purposeful response
Moderate sedation; any movement to pain counts as purposeful
Minimal sedation; he responded to touch
Moderate sedation, since he is still breathing on his own with support
questions.explanation: Purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation defines deep sedation; reflex withdrawal alone does not count, so he may be at GA. Moderate sedation requires purposeful response to voice or light touch, and spontaneous breathing does not define the level.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: You are titrating propofol for an ERCP. The patient now needs jaw thrust, then stops responding to a sternal rub, and BP drifts from 132/80 to 104/62. Using the ASA continuum, which function is the LAST to be described as possibly impaired, and at what level?
options: Cardiovascular function, at general anesthesia
Cardiovascular function, at deep sedation
Spontaneous ventilation, at moderate sedation
Airway patency, at minimal sedation
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular function is usually maintained through deep sedation and is described as possibly impaired only at GA. Ventilation becomes possibly inadequate earlier, at deep sedation, and the airway may need intervention there.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: Three patients are sedated for colonoscopy. Patient A answers questions normally. Patient B opens her eyes when you say her name loudly. Patient C responds only after a sternal rub and needs a chin lift to stop snoring. Which patient is at the FIRST level where airway intervention may be required?
options: Patient C, at deep sedation
Patient B, at moderate sedation
Patient A, at minimal sedation
None of them, because airway intervention begins at GA
questions.explanation: Airway intervention "may be required" first appears at deep sedation (patient C). Moderate sedation (patient B) requires no intervention, minimal sedation (A) leaves the airway unaffected, and at GA intervention is often required.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: A patient answers questions appropriately after midazolam 1 mg but cannot touch finger to nose smoothly. SpO2 99%, RR 14. Which level best fits?
options: Minimal sedation, since coordination may be impaired
Moderate sedation, since coordination is impaired
Deep sedation, since motor function is depressed
Minimal sedation, as long as coordination is intact
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation allows impaired cognition and coordination while ventilation and cardiovascular function remain unaffected. Impaired coordination alone does not move the patient to moderate sedation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old receives oral midazolam before an MRI for claustrophobia. She is calm, talks normally, and her SpO2 is 99% on room air. Which outcome would mean the plan has exceeded its goal?
options: She stops responding normally to conversation
She reports feeling less anxious about the scanner
She keeps a normal respiratory rate and SpO2
She remembers parts of the procedure afterward
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation aims to reduce anxiety while keeping normal response to voice and intact protective reflexes. Losing normal conversational response means she has moved to moderate sedation. Reduced anxiety, normal breathing, and some recall are all consistent with the goal.

questions.stem: Under propofol for a dressing change, a patient becomes apneic for 20 seconds at a time, his ETCO2 rises to 62 on brief breaths, and he does not withdraw purposefully to pain. Which ventilation descriptor and level fit?
options: Ventilation frequently inadequate, at general anesthesia
Ventilation may be inadequate, at deep sedation with a jaw thrust
Ventilation adequate, at moderate sedation
Ventilation unaffected, at minimal sedation
questions.explanation: "Frequently inadequate" ventilation belongs to GA, which also fits his lack of purposeful response to pain. Deep sedation is "may be inadequate," moderate is "adequate," and minimal is "unaffected."

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: You plan moderate sedation with midazolam and fentanyl for a TEE in a 68-year-old with OSA. What rescue capability must you have before starting?
options: Rescue from deep sedation, one level beyond the plan
Rescue from moderate sedation, the planned level
Rescue from minimal sedation, matching the oral premedication
Airway rescue by the code team, called when needed
questions.explanation: Because depth moves along a continuum, a provider must be able to rescue a patient from the next deeper level. Planning only for the intended level, or relying on others for rescue, misses that principle.

questions.stem: During a TEE under propofol sedation, the patient obstructs and you need a sustained jaw thrust to restore airflow. What does needing this maneuver tell you about your preparedness obligations?
options: You must be ready to manage GA, including laryngoscopy
You should now proceed with routine intubation
A secured airway should have been placed before starting
Laryngoscopy is the first move for any obstruction
questions.explanation: Needing jaw thrust puts the patient at deep sedation, one step from GA, so the provider must be able to rescue from GA. That does not mean every deeply sedated patient is intubated.

questions.stem: A patient under moderate sedation for colonoscopy is conversing between boluses. Twenty minutes later, as the scope reaches the cecum and stimulation drops, she is snoring with an SpO2 of 91%. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Depth shifts quickly with drug peaks and changing stimulation
Moderate sedation requires continuous core temperature monitoring
Cardiovascular function is usually impaired at moderate depth
Propofol accumulates once the infusion passes 20 minutes
questions.explanation: Depth moves as boluses peak and stimulation rises and falls, which is why moderate sedation requires continuous reassessment. Patients at moderate depth can still respond, and cardiovascular function is usually maintained.

questions.stem: Patient A responds purposefully when you call his name and breathes adequately without help. Patient B responds only after repeated painful stimulation and needs a jaw thrust to keep SpO2 above 92%. Which statement correctly separates them?
options: A is moderate with no airway intervention; B is deep and may need it
A is minimal and B is moderate, since both respond to stimulation
A and B are both deep, since both need stimulation
A is deep and B is general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation means purposeful response to voice or light touch with no airway intervention. Deep sedation means purposeful response only after repeated or painful stimulation, with airway intervention possibly required.

questions.stem: A patient at planned moderate sedation stops answering questions but grimaces and says "ow" with a firm sternal rub. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: He is now deeply sedated and airway readiness must increase
He remains moderately sedated because he spoke
He is under general anesthesia because he needed a painful stimulus
He is minimally sedated because he can still speak
questions.explanation: Purposeful response only after painful stimulation places him in deep sedation, beyond the intended level. That change should trigger closer airway and ventilation monitoring and a readiness to support.

questions.stem: A patient under midazolam and fentanyl keeps her eyes closed but opens them and squeezes your hand when you tap her shoulder and say her name. Her respiratory rate is 12 and capnography is normal. How is she classified?
options: Moderate sedation, also called conscious sedation
Minimal sedation, since she follows a command
Deep sedation, since her eyes are closed
General anesthesia, since she needed touch
questions.explanation: Purposeful response to verbal or light tactile stimulation is moderate ("conscious") sedation. Closed eyes do not change the level; the type of stimulus needed and the response do.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: A 64-year-old under propofol sedation for a cystoscopy coughs weakly when secretions pool, then stops coughing entirely as you deepen the infusion. What does this progression illustrate?
options: Protective airway reflexes fade progressively with depth
Airway reflexes stay intact until general anesthesia
Airway reflexes disappear at minimal sedation
Airway reflexes strengthen as sedation deepens
questions.explanation: The ASA continuum describes progressive impairment of responsiveness, protective reflexes, ventilation, and cardiovascular function as depth increases. The loss is gradual rather than a single cutoff.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receives midazolam 2 mg, which alone barely affects his breathing, then fentanyl 50 mcg, which alone would also be tolerated. Two minutes later his respiratory rate is 4. What best explains this?
options: The drugs' respiratory depression is synergistic, not just additive
Fentanyl's peak effect arrived later than midazolam's
Fentanyl's chest wall rigidity is preventing breathing
Midazolam's effect peaked late and caused this by itself
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines and opioids depress ventilation synergistically, so their combined effect is greater than the sum of each. Low-dose fentanyl rarely causes rigidity, and an allergy would not present this way.

questions.stem: A patient under propofol for a cardioversion moans and pulls away only after a sternal rub, and her SpO2 falls to 91% until a jaw thrust is applied. BP is 118/72, unchanged from baseline. Which statements describe her state? (Select 2)
options: She is not easily aroused
Her ability to maintain ventilation may be impaired
Spontaneous ventilation is reliably adequate without support
No airway intervention should be required
Cardiovascular function is usually impaired at this level
She has a normal response to verbal commands
questions.explanation: She is at deep sedation: not easily aroused, with ventilation possibly impaired and airway help needed. Cardiovascular function is usually maintained at this level, as her stable BP shows.

questions.stem: A patient is under moderate sedation with midazolam and fentanyl for a bronchoscopy-adjacent ENT procedure. Which statements apply to this level of sedation? (Select 4)
options: Continuous capnography is required
Spontaneous ventilation should remain adequate
The goal is a patient who still responds purposefully
No airway intervention should routinely be needed
Cardiovascular function is frequently impaired
Pulse oximetry alone is enough to monitor ventilation
questions.explanation: At moderate sedation the patient responds purposefully, ventilation stays adequate, and no airway intervention is required. Capnography is required, and cardiovascular function is usually maintained.

questions.stem: A patient receiving propofol for EGD no longer responds to her name. What should the provider recognize?
options: Sedation may now carry the risk profile of general anesthesia
She has reached ideal moderate sedation for EGD
Propofol has produced analgesia sufficient for biopsy
Verbal response is lost first but reflexes stay protected
questions.explanation: The propofol slide warns that loss of verbal responsiveness means sedation may be approaching GA with an unprotected airway. Propofol does not provide analgesia.

questions.stem: Before an endoscopy, a patient receives a low dose of midazolam and chats normally. Her BP falls from 132/80 to 104/60. How should you interpret this change?
options: Unexpected, since cardiovascular function should be unaffected at minimal sedation
Expected, since minimal sedation usually impairs cardiovascular function
Expected, since cardiovascular function may be impaired at minimal sedation
Expected, since midazolam vasodilates even at minimal sedation
questions.explanation: At minimal sedation, cardiovascular function is unaffected. A 20% BP drop at this level should prompt a search for another cause, such as hypovolemia or vagal response.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: Which pairing of sedation level and airway descriptor matches the ASA continuum?
options: General anesthesia: intervention often required
Deep sedation: no intervention required
Moderate sedation: intervention may be required
Minimal sedation: intervention often required
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation leaves the airway unaffected, moderate requires no intervention, deep may require it, and GA often requires it.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: During deep sedation for cardioversion, which finding is still considered "usually maintained" on the ASA table?
options: Cardiovascular function
Spontaneous ventilation
Airway patency without support
Normal response to voice
questions.explanation: At deep sedation, cardiovascular function is usually maintained, while ventilation may be inadequate and the airway may need intervention. Normal response to voice belongs to minimal sedation.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: You plan only minimal sedation with oral midazolam for an anxious patient having a skin biopsy under local. Which rescue must you be prepared for before giving the drug?
options: Rescue from moderate sedation
Rescue from minimal sedation, the planned level
Rescue from general anesthesia
No rescue planning, since oral midazolam is mild
questions.explanation: You must be able to rescue a patient from the level beyond your target. For planned minimal sedation, that is moderate sedation.

questions.stem: Under propofol, a patient does not respond to a sternal rub or trapezius squeeze, needs a chin lift, and has a respiratory rate of 6. Which responsiveness descriptor fits his level?
options: Unarousable even with painful stimulation
Purposeful response after repeated painful stimulation
Purposeful response to verbal or light tactile stimulation
Normal response to verbal stimulation
questions.explanation: Being unarousable even to painful stimulation defines GA. Purposeful response after repeated or painful stimulation is deep sedation.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: Two hours into a moderate-sedation case, a 50-year-old becomes restless, keeps moving under the drapes, and tries to remove the nasal cannula. The proceduralist asks for "a little more." What is the main risk of responding with additional boluses?
options: The patient slides into deeper-than-intended sedation
Emergence delirium that prevents further sedation
Paradoxical agitation from the midazolam already given
Hypertension that will require beta blockade
questions.explanation: Long cases bring restlessness and disinhibition, which prompt more drug and raise the chance of deeper-than-intended sedation with an unsecured airway. Disinhibition can itself be a sign of oversedation.

questions.stem: Under sedation, a patient pulls her hand away when you pinch it but does not look at you, speak, or reach toward the stimulus. Repeated stimulation gives the same result. What does this response indicate?
options: She has passed beyond deep sedation, since withdrawal is reflexive
She is at deep sedation, since she responds to painful stimulation
She is at moderate sedation, since she moved
She is at minimal sedation, since she withdrew
questions.explanation: Reflex withdrawal is not a purposeful response. Deep sedation requires purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation, so a reflex-only response places her at GA.

questions.stem: A GI nurse's protocol says "conscious sedation" for colonoscopy. Under the ASA definitions, which level does this term describe, and what airway support should it require?
options: Moderate sedation, with no airway intervention required
Minimal sedation, with an unaffected airway
Deep sedation, with airway intervention possibly required
Any level of sedation, depending on the drug
questions.explanation: Conscious sedation is synonymous with moderate sedation/analgesia, which requires no airway intervention. If the patient needs airway support, he has moved beyond the intended level.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: You give identical 30 mg propofol boluses every 3 minutes during an ERCP. The first two keep the patient at moderate sedation, but after the third she suddenly needs a jaw thrust. What principle explains this?
options: Depth moves along a continuum without clear boundaries between levels
Each bolus produces the same fixed depth
Propofol accumulates after the fifth bolus in most patients
Depth depends on the drug chosen and not on the cumulative dose given
questions.explanation: Sedation is a continuum, so cumulative dosing and changing stimulation can shift a patient across levels without warning.

questions.stem: A patient at deep sedation for joint reduction has RR 7 with shallow breaths. Per the ASA table, this finding is:
options: An expected possibility that may need support
Unexpected and signals general anesthesia
Normal because ventilation is unaffected
Expected only at general anesthesia, not deep sedation
questions.explanation: Spontaneous ventilation "may be inadequate" at deep sedation. It is an anticipated risk requiring assessment and support, not proof of GA.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: A patient goes from talking normally, to responding when called, to responding only to a sternal rub, to no response at all. Which sequence names those levels in order?
options: Minimal, moderate, deep, general anesthesia
Moderate, minimal, deep, general anesthesia
Minimal, deep, moderate, general anesthesia
Anxiolysis, deep, moderate, general anesthesia
questions.explanation: The ASA continuum runs minimal (anxiolysis), moderate (conscious sedation), deep, and general anesthesia.

questions.stem: At the start of a colonoscopy, a patient answered when called. Twenty minutes later she responds only after you shake her shoulder several times. Her respiratory rate is 10. What should you conclude?
options: She has likely moved to deep sedation; reassess and hold further drug
She is still at moderate sedation; continue the plan as written
She is at minimal sedation, since she responded
She is at general anesthesia, since she needed touch
questions.explanation: Response only after repeated stimulation suggests deep sedation. Hold further sedative, reassess ventilation, and be ready to support the airway.

questions.stem: Which of the following apply at general anesthesia on the ASA continuum? (Select 4)
options: Unarousable even to painful stimulus
Airway intervention often required
Cardiovascular function may be impaired
Spontaneous ventilation is frequently inadequate
Purposeful response after repeated stimulation
Cardiovascular function is unaffected
questions.explanation: At GA, patients are unarousable, need airway intervention often, have frequently inadequate ventilation, and may have impaired cardiovascular function.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: Two patients receive midazolam before a cataract case. Patient A talks and answers normally. Patient B is drowsy and answers only when you speak to her directly. What separates their levels?
options: A responds normally (minimal); B responds purposefully but not normally (moderate)
A is moderate and B is deep
Both are minimal, since both answer questions when spoken to
Both are moderate, since both received midazolam and both answer questions when spoken to
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation keeps a normal response to voice; moderate sedation keeps a purposeful but diminished response.

questions.stem: The notes on the continuum slide warn about GI suites. What is the specific risk mentioned?
options: Aspiration from abdominal pressure on the stomach
Hypothermia from prolonged bowel preparation
Hypotension from vasovagal response to insufflation
Laryngospasm from the endoscope at the cords
questions.explanation: The handwritten note flags aspiration from pushing on the stomach in the GI suite. Abdominal pressure during colonoscopy can push gastric contents up in a patient with impaired reflexes.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: A patient receives dexmedetomidine and ketamine for an abscess drainage. He responds purposefully to his name but is slow. The procedure becomes more stimulating. What is the MOST likely next change?
options: More stimulation lightens him, prompting more drug and deeper risk
More stimulation deepens him without added drug
Ketamine holds him at a fixed depth whatever the stimulus
Dexmedetomidine's alpha-2 effect will hold him at his current depth
questions.explanation: Titration must match changing procedural stimulus. Intense stimulation often lightens the patient and prompts extra dosing, and depth can overshoot once the stimulus ends.

questions.stem: Which finding BEST tells you a patient has moved from minimal to moderate sedation?
options: He answers only when spoken to directly, not in normal conversation
He reports feeling relaxed
His respiratory rate is 14 with a normal capnogram waveform
His BP is unchanged from baseline and his heart rate is stable
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation is purposeful but not normal response to voice. Relaxation, normal breathing, and stable BP all fit minimal sedation as well.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with an EF of 25% is deeply sedated for a TEE. Her BP falls from 110/70 to 78/42. A trainee says, "Deep sedation usually maintains cardiovascular function, so this must be equipment error." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: "Usually maintained" does not protect patients with limited reserve
Cardiovascular function is usually impaired at deep sedation
The cuff is likely too large for her arm
She has moved to minimal sedation as the drug wore off
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular function is usually maintained at deep sedation, but patients with limited reserve can still become unstable. Treat the hypotension and check the patient first.

questions.stem: You are planning sedation for four cases today: electrical cardioversion, routine colonoscopy, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and image-guided biopsy. Which case will usually require a brief period of deep sedation?
options: Electrical cardioversion
Routine colonoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Image-guided liver biopsy
questions.explanation: Cardioversion is intensely stimulating but very short, so it is usually done under brief deep sedation. The other procedures are commonly done at minimal to moderate depth in selected patients.

questions.stem: During a long sedation case, a patient goes from answering to her name, to responding only to repeated shaking, to moaning without purposeful movement even with a jaw thrust. How many levels has she moved?
options: Two levels, from moderate sedation to general anesthesia
One level, from moderate to deep sedation
One level, from minimal to moderate sedation
Three levels, from minimal sedation to general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Answering to her name is moderate; responding only to repeated stimulation is deep; no purposeful response is GA.

questions.stem: A protocol lists "anxiolysis" as the plan for a dental patient. Which response to voice and airway state should this patient have?
options: Normal response to voice with an unaffected airway
Purposeful response with no airway intervention needed
Response after repeated stimulation, airway possibly at risk
No response, with airway intervention often required
questions.explanation: Anxiolysis is minimal sedation, with normal response to verbal stimulation and an unaffected airway.

questions.stem: During a fracture reduction, a patient grimaced and pushed your hand away from the injury when you pressed on it. After another propofol bolus, he no longer reacts to the same pressure. What does this change mark?
options: Transition from deep sedation to general anesthesia
Transition from moderate to deep sedation
Transition from minimal to moderate sedation
No change in level, since he is still breathing spontaneously
questions.explanation: Loss of purposeful response to painful stimulation marks the move from deep sedation to GA.

questions.stem: During a deep sedation case for a painful dressing change, the patient's respiratory rate falls to 4 and he no longer withdraws to painful stimulation. What state has he entered, and what must you be prepared to do?
options: General anesthesia; rescue the airway and ventilation
Moderate sedation; lighten the infusion and observe
Emergence delirium; give a benzodiazepine
Local anesthetic toxicity; give lipid emulsion
questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness to painful stimulation with inadequate ventilation is general anesthesia. Anyone providing deep sedation must be able to rescue a patient who enters GA.

questions.stem: A patient under propofol is quiet and still with a regular breathing pattern. The proceduralist says, "She's at moderate sedation." What must you do to confirm her level?
options: Stimulate her and observe her response
Rely on the steady breathing pattern
Check that her SpO2 is above 95%
Rely on the dose given so far
questions.explanation: Depth is defined by response to stimulation. Without stimulating, you cannot tell moderate from deep sedation or GA; breathing pattern, SpO2, and dose do not define the level.

questions.stem: A patient under moderate sedation looks comfortable with regular chest movement. What is the BEST way to confirm that her ventilation is adequate?
options: Continuous capnography
Pulse oximetry on supplemental oxygen
Visual inspection of chest movement alone
Her ability to respond to her name
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation should keep ventilation adequate, but capnography confirms it. SpO2 lags on supplemental oxygen, and chest movement can occur with obstruction.

questions.stem: A patient's response to name is intact, but her RR has dropped from 16 to 6 with ETCO2 rising. What BEST describes the situation?
options: Responsiveness and ventilation are diverging; treat the ventilation
She remains at moderate sedation, so no action is needed now
She is at GA because her ventilation is now inadequate
Rising ETCO2 means she is lightening from the sedation
questions.explanation: Depth labels are based on responsiveness, but ventilation can fail at any depth, especially with opioids. Treat the hypoventilation first.

questions.stem: During a TEE, a patient moves from moderate to deep sedation. Which ASA descriptor is the SAME at both levels?
options: Cardiovascular function usually maintained
Response to voice
Need for airway intervention
Adequacy of spontaneous ventilation without support
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular function is usually maintained at both moderate and deep sedation. Responsiveness, airway, and ventilation all worsen.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: You plan brief deep sedation with propofol for an elective cardioversion. Which equipment must be ready before induction?
options: Full airway rescue equipment, including laryngoscopy
Nasal cannula, suction, and an oral airway at the bedside
A bag-mask device and oral airway
Equipment for minimal sedation kept nearby
questions.explanation: Deep sedation requires readiness to rescue from GA, which means full airway equipment including laryngoscopy and advanced airways.

questions.stem: A patient at deep sedation stops breathing for 30 seconds but responds to a sternal rub by taking a breath and moaning. Which level best fits?
options: Deep sedation with inadequate ventilation
Moderate sedation with intact ventilation
Minimal sedation with a vasovagal response
General anesthesia with preserved reflexes
questions.explanation: Moaning and breathing with pain can be a purposeful response, placing her in deep sedation, where ventilation may be inadequate. Apnea still requires intervention.

questions.stem: During a single procedure, a patient's responsiveness, airway reflexes, ventilation, and then BP decline as more drug is given. Which model describes this pattern?
options: A continuum where function declines as depth increases
A scale defined by processed EEG values
A classification used outside the operating room
A fixed set of separate, stable levels
questions.explanation: The ASA describes sedation as a continuum where responsiveness, airway, ventilation, and cardiovascular function progressively decline.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old receives oral midazolam before a cataract case. She is calm, answers questions normally, and breathes without assistance. Which airway description fits this level of sedation?
options: Airway unaffected, as expected at minimal sedation
No intervention required, as described for moderate sedation
Intervention may be required, as at deep sedation
Airway likely needs intervention, as at GA
questions.explanation: Only minimal sedation describes the airway as unaffected. Moderate sedation is "no intervention required," which is not the same as unaffected.

image.title: ASA continuum of depth of sedation

questions.stem: A patient becomes unresponsive to voice but opens eyes and says "stop" with a firm trapezius squeeze. You were planning moderate sedation. What is the FIRST action?
options: Assess airway and ventilation and stop further dosing
Give flumazenil to restore moderate sedation
Proceed, since a purposeful response is still present
Intubate because deep sedation was not planned
questions.explanation: She has moved into deep sedation. The first step is assessing airway and ventilation and holding further drug while supporting as needed.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with a short neck and limited mouth opening is booked for EGD with propofol sedation. Before you draw up any drug, what is the key planning question?
options: Can I ventilate or intubate if sedation goes deeper than planned?
Will this patient remember the procedure afterward?
Is the gastroenterologist comfortable with the sedation depth?
Will the patient tolerate supplemental oxygen during the case?
questions.explanation: Every sedation plan starts with whether you can rescue the airway if depth overshoots. A difficult-looking airway makes that question the deciding factor in the plan.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old for EGD has Mallampati III, full dentition, and good mouth opening. Which additional exam finding would MOST raise concern about rescue if sedation deepens?
options: Thyromental distance of two fingerbreadths
Capillary refill under two seconds
Mild jugular venous distension when supine
A soft left carotid bruit
questions.explanation: A short thyromental distance predicts difficult laryngoscopy and adds to Mallampati III. The other findings do not predict airway difficulty.

questions.stem: Using LEMON on a patient for sedation, you find a receding chin and measure two fingerbreadths of mouth opening and two from mentum to hyoid. Which LEMON letter does this measurement address?
options: E: evaluate the 3-3-2 rule
L: look externally at the face and neck
M: Mallampati classification
N: neck mobility
questions.explanation: LEMON stands for Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2, Mallampati, Obstruction, Neck mobility. Fingerbreadth measurements belong to the 3-3-2 evaluation.

questions.stem: During a 3-3-2 assessment, you can fit only two fingers between the patient's incisors. What does this finding predict?
options: Limited mouth opening that hinders laryngoscopy and airway devices
A short mandibular space that limits tongue displacement on DL
A high larynx relative to the base of the tongue
Limited neck extension for the sniffing position
questions.explanation: The first "3" measures mouth opening; fewer than three fingerbreadths limits laryngoscope and device insertion. The second 3 measures the mandibular space, and the 2 measures larynx position.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with severe OSA, BMI 42, and Mallampati IV is scheduled for EGD with deep sedation. Which LEMON element does the OSA itself address?
options: Obstruction
Look externally
Mallampati score
Neck mobility
questions.explanation: O in LEMON is obstruction, which includes sleep apnea, enlarged tonsils, and tumors. Mallampati and neck mobility are assessed separately.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for MAC says, "Last time they told me I was hard to wake up and had trouble breathing on the mask." Why does this history matter most for your plan?
options: It predicts difficult rescue if sedation becomes too deep
It predicts a higher propofol dose requirement today
It means sedation is contraindicated for this patient today
It predicts postoperative nausea and vomiting
questions.explanation: A history of difficult mask ventilation, difficult intubation, or OSA predicts difficulty rescuing the airway if sedation overshoots. It shapes drug choice, depth, and backup equipment.

questions.stem: You are setting up for moderate sedation in a healthy patient. When should oxygen delivery and rescue devices be planned and checked?
options: Before any sedative is given
When the patient first desaturates
When a difficult airway is predicted
After the proceduralist starts
questions.explanation: Oxygen and rescue equipment must be ready before any sedative, because depth can change quickly even in healthy patients.

questions.stem: A patient with gastroparesis is scheduled for EGD under sedation. Why does aspiration risk make him a high-caution patient?
options: Sedation blunts protective reflexes while the airway stays unprotected
Sedatives increase gastric acid production
Sedation stops gastric emptying and raises gastric volume
Aspiration risk rules out sedation entirely for this patient and procedure
questions.explanation: Sedation impairs protective reflexes without securing the airway. Aspiration risk calls for caution and may push the plan toward GA, but it does not forbid sedation.

questions.stem: Four patients are scheduled for sedation. Which needs the LEAST added caution?
options: A 40-year-old ASA I with a normal airway exam
A 70-year-old taking clonazepam nightly
A patient with cirrhosis and ascites
A patient with bulbar weakness after a stroke
questions.explanation: Chronic benzodiazepine use, hepatic dysfunction, and neurologic disease affecting airway reflexes all require extra caution. A healthy ASA I with a normal airway does not.

questions.stem: A patient who drinks heavily daily and takes alprazolam needs more midazolam than expected, then becomes apneic after a small additional dose. What explains this?
options: Chronic exposure alters dose needs and makes response unpredictable
Alcohol reduces the risk of respiratory depression
Tolerance means sedative doses can be increased without risk
Benzodiazepine use protects against oversedation from propofol
questions.explanation: Chronic benzodiazepine or alcohol exposure creates tolerance and an unpredictable response, so titrate carefully.

questions.stem: A patient with CKD stage 4 and cirrhosis receives a standard midazolam dose and remains sedated for hours. What explains this?
options: Altered drug disposition from renal and hepatic dysfunction
Increased drug absorption from the GI tract
Increased receptor tolerance to midazolam from chronic illness
Tolerance from chronic illness altering receptor sensitivity
questions.explanation: Renal and hepatic dysfunction alter metabolism and clearance of sedatives and their active metabolites, prolonging effects.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with Parkinson's disease and dysphagia is booked for EGD sedation. Which caution category applies MOST directly?
options: Neurologic disease affecting airway reflexes
Chronic sedative or opioid use
Renal or hepatic dysfunction
Uncooperative or unwilling patient behavior
questions.explanation: Parkinson's with dysphagia impairs swallowing and airway protection, raising aspiration and obstruction risk.

questions.stem: You are reviewing tomorrow's sedation list. Which patients call for extra caution? (Select 4)
options: A man whose wife reports loud snoring and witnessed apneas
A frail 88-year-old with limited reserve
An uncooperative patient who refuses to stay still
A patient on long-term oxycodone
A healthy 30-year-old with a normal airway
A patient with mild seasonal allergies
questions.explanation: Suspected sleep apnea, frailty, uncooperative behavior, and chronic opioid use all call for extra caution.

questions.stem: During a LEMON assessment, you note a full beard, a small mandible, and facial trauma. Which LEMON element captures these findings?
options: L: look externally
E: evaluate 3-3-2
M: Mallampati
O: obstruction
questions.explanation: Visible external features such as beards, a small mandible, and facial trauma fall under "look externally."

questions.stem: During the airway exam, the patient cannot slide the lower incisors forward past the upper incisors. What does this finding predict during sedation?
options: Jaw thrust and laryngoscopy may be difficult
Mask seal will be easier than average
Neck extension will be limited
Mallampati class will improve with phonation
questions.explanation: Limited mandibular protrusion means poor mandibular mobility. It predicts difficulty with jaw thrust and with displacing the tongue during laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated OSA desaturates repeatedly during light sedation for a colonoscopy, although her ventilatory drive is intact. What is the MAIN mechanism?
options: Sedatives reduce pharyngeal muscle tone and worsen upper airway collapse
Sedatives cause bronchospasm in OSA
OSA patients have reduced oxygen-carrying capacity from polycythemia
Sedatives raise CO2 production in OSA
questions.explanation: Sedatives decrease upper airway muscle tone, which worsens collapse in patients with OSA.

questions.stem: A patient with a Mallampati IV and limited mouth opening requests deep sedation for EGD. What is the BEST first step?
options: Plan a conversion-to-GA and airway rescue strategy before starting
Proceed with titrated propofol since EGD is brief and stimulating
Give minimal sedation and accept poor tolerance of the scope
Intubate awake before sedation for every EGD patient
questions.explanation: The lecture says develop a conversion plan before starting and plan rescue devices before medications. Airway findings shape the plan rather than automatically cancelling.

questions.stem: In Scenario 1, the cataract patient lies flat with drapes over her face. Which finding from her assessment is the MOST important airway concern?
options: Mallampati III with limited neck extension
Controlled hypertension
Mild anxiety about the procedure
A short planned procedure time under 20 minutes
questions.explanation: Mallampati III and limited neck extension predict difficult rescue, made worse by limited access under the drapes.

questions.stem: Two patients have the same procedure. One is a frail 89-year-old with an EF of 30%; the other is a fit 45-year-old. Which caution category applies to the first patient?
options: Advanced age, frailty, or limited reserve
Chronic sedative or opioid use
Neurologic disease affecting airway reflexes
Uncooperative or unwilling patient
questions.explanation: Advanced age, frailty, and limited cardiopulmonary reserve increase sensitivity to sedatives and reduce tolerance of hypotension or hypoxemia.

questions.stem: A healthy patient is scheduled for minimal sedation with oral midazolam. Is a pre-sedation airway assessment needed?
options: Yes, because depth can exceed the plan at any level
No, it is needed for planned deep sedation
No, it is needed when OSA is documented
No, oral premedication stays within minimal sedation
questions.explanation: The pre-sedation airway assessment is always performed, because any sedative can produce deeper sedation than intended.

questions.stem: A seated patient opens her mouth and protrudes her tongue without phonating, and you see only the soft palate and the base of the uvula. What does this exam assess?
options: Visibility of oropharyngeal structures relative to tongue size
Mouth opening in fingerbreadths
Mandibular protrusion of the lower incisors past the upper incisors
Thyromental distance with the head fully extended
questions.explanation: The Mallampati exam assesses oropharyngeal visibility, an indirect measure of tongue size relative to the oral cavity. This view is class III.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old has BMI 27, no OSA, a normal airway, and previously tolerated colonoscopy poorly. What does the poor prior tolerance MOST suggest?
options: Higher analgesic or sedative need than typical
A contraindication to sedation
An undiagnosed difficult airway
Need for general endotracheal anesthesia this time
questions.explanation: Poor tolerance suggests stimulation exceeds what light sedation covers. It predicts higher drug needs, which increases respiratory risk.

questions.stem: Which caution list items would apply to the Scenario 3 EGD patient? (Select 3)
options: Aspiration risk
Obesity or difficult airway features
OSA
Chronic benzodiazepine exposure
Renal dysfunction altering drug disposition
Uncooperative behavior
questions.explanation: BMI 42, severe OSA, regurgitation when flat, and Mallampati IV map to obesity/difficult airway, OSA, and aspiration risk.

questions.stem: During a LEMON assessment, a patient with ankylosing spondylitis cannot extend his neck or flex it forward. Which letter applies, and why does it matter?
options: N: neck mobility, which limits positioning for laryngoscopy
L: look externally, which predicts mask difficulty
E: 3-3-2, which measures mouth opening
O: obstruction, which suggests a mass or tumor in the airway
questions.explanation: Neck mobility assesses flexion and extension needed for the sniffing position and laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old with severe claustrophobia refuses to lie still for an MRI and repeatedly sits up in the scanner. How should this factor shape your plan?
options: Treat non-cooperation as a patient caution and plan deeper care
Treat it as a procedure issue rather than a patient factor
Treat it as a contraindication to any anesthesia care
Treat it as a reason to keep sedation minimal
questions.explanation: Non-cooperative or unwilling patients need more caution, and procedures requiring immobility make cooperation essential. This often pushes the plan toward deeper sedation or GA with a protected airway.

questions.stem: In Scenario 3, the patient with a BMI of 42 and severe OSA also takes weekly semaglutide. Which additional risk does semaglutide add?
options: Higher aspiration risk from delayed gastric emptying
Greater hemodynamic instability from GLP-1 effects on volume
Greater sensitivity to propofol
Increased bleeding risk
questions.explanation: GLP-1 agonists delay gastric emptying, adding aspiration risk to his existing OSA and airway concerns.

questions.stem: A patient with OSA who does not use home CPAP will undergo cataract surgery under MAC. Which position concern is MOST relevant?
options: Supine position may worsen airway obstruction
Prone positioning limits airway access
Beach chair alters cerebral autoregulation
Lateral position reduces dependent-lung FRC
questions.explanation: The lecture states supine increases airway obstruction, especially in obesity and OSA. Cataract surgery is done supine.

questions.stem: A morbidly obese patient with OSA is scheduled for MAC. Which question should drive your equipment and backup plan?
options: What will I do if this patient needs full ventilatory support?
How quickly can I bring this patient to a deep, comfortable level?
How much midazolam can I give before he falls asleep?
Can the proceduralist add more local later?
questions.explanation: Airway planning for sedation centers on rescue if sedation overshoots. In obesity and OSA, that means immediate means to ventilate and intubate.

questions.stem: You are performing a pre-sedation airway exam in a patient scheduled for EGD. Which findings belong in that exam? (Select 5)
options: Mouth opening
Dentition
Neck range of motion
Mandibular mobility
Thyromental distance
Peak expiratory flow
questions.explanation: The pre-sedation airway exam includes mouth opening, dentition, Mallampati, mandibular mobility, neck range of motion, and thyromental distance. Peak flow is a pulmonary test, not part of the airway exam.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with severe OSA desaturated to 78% during propofol sedation last year and now needs a bronchoscopy. Which change in drug choice is BEST?
options: Use an agent with less respiratory depression, such as dexmedetomidine
Use larger propofol boluses to shorten the case and exposure
Add fentanyl to propofol so lower propofol doses can be used for the case
Use midazolam alone, since it spares ventilation
questions.explanation: Severe OSA with prior desaturation favors an agent with minimal respiratory depression. Synergistic combinations and larger boluses increase risk, and midazolam still depresses ventilation.

questions.stem: You need sedation for a bronchoscopy in a patient with cirrhosis, CKD stage 4, and severe OSA. Why might remimazolam be preferred over midazolam?
options: Its tissue esterase metabolism avoids hepatic and renal accumulation
It provides analgesia that spares opioids
It provides analgesia that lets you cut opioid doses
Its effect is not reversed by flumazenil, so offset is predictable
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is broken down by tissue esterases, so it does not accumulate in liver or kidney failure. It still depresses breathing, provides no analgesia, and is reversible with flumazenil.

questions.stem: During a LEMON assessment, a child has 3+ tonsils and loud snoring with witnessed apneas. Which LEMON element do these findings fall under?
options: O: obstruction
L: look externally
E: evaluate 3-3-2
N: neck mobility
questions.explanation: Obstruction covers enlarged tonsils, oral pathology, sleep apnea, and tumors that can block the airway.

questions.stem: A frail 88-year-old with an ejection fraction of 30% needs a closed shoulder reduction under sedation. Which approach is BEST?
options: Reduce doses and titrate slowly with close monitoring
Use standard adult doses for a predictable effect
Avoid sedation entirely in a frail patient
Give one large bolus to shorten the exposure time
questions.explanation: Age and limited cardiac reserve strongly increase drug effect and slow circulation time. Small, slowly titrated doses with close monitoring are safer than standard or bolus dosing.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with pulmonary hypertension (PASP 70 mmHg) and COPD is scheduled for TEE under MAC. How should the pulmonary hypertension shape your plan?
options: It is a high-risk condition; avoid hypoxemia and hypercarbia
It allows minimal sedation without capnography monitoring
It is a contraindication to capnography
It requires switching to an inhaled anesthetic
questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension is a key risk condition in MAC preop assessment. Hypoxemia and hypercarbia from oversedation raise PVR and can precipitate right heart failure.

questions.stem: Four sedation patients have different airway findings. Which combination makes bag-mask ventilation MOST difficult if rescue is needed?
options: A full beard with OSA
Mallampati II with full dentition
A thyromental distance of 7 cm
Normal neck extension in a thin patient
questions.explanation: Facial hair prevents a mask seal and OSA predicts obstruction, both predictors of difficult BMV. The other findings are reassuring.

questions.stem: You are planning sedation for two cases: a superficial skin biopsy and a percutaneous liver ablation. What should you estimate from each procedure to choose drugs and depth?
options: The analgesic requirement from the procedural stimulus
The expected blood product requirement for the case
The total intravenous fluid requirement
The supplemental oxygen flow requirement
questions.explanation: Estimating the analgesic requirement from the expected stimulus drives drug choice and planned depth. A liver ablation needs far more analgesia than a skin biopsy.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia is scheduled for a carotid stent under sedation, and the neurointerventionalist needs him to squeeze a hand on command. What must be assessed preoperatively?
options: His ability to cooperate with neurologic testing
Nothing more, since deep sedation will be used
His score on a pediatric cooperation scale
His processed EEG baseline before sedation
questions.explanation: Ability to cooperate is part of the preop assessment, and procedures needing patient cooperation or neurologic checks depend on it. If he cannot cooperate, the plan may need to change.

questions.stem: A patient with morbid obesity will be placed supine for a 90-minute procedure under MAC. Which combination raises risk the MOST?
options: Supine obstruction plus a long unsecured-airway exposure
Beach chair plus short duration
Lateral position plus minimal sedation
Prone position with a secured airway for a long case
questions.explanation: Supine increases obstruction in obesity, and long procedures add exposure to an unsecured airway and restless, deeper-than-intended sedation.

questions.stem: Four patients are scheduled for EGD. Which one MOST strongly argues for GA with a secured airway rather than MAC?
options: Active regurgitation, severe OSA, and Mallampati IV
Controlled hypertension and mild anxiety
A healthy 35-year-old with dyspepsia
A 60-year-old with stable asthma on an inhaler
questions.explanation: Active regurgitation with a difficult airway and OSA combines high aspiration risk with difficult rescue. A protected airway is safer.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old and a 40-year-old receive the same propofol dose. The older patient becomes hypotensive and apneic. Why does advanced age belong on the caution list?
options: Reduced reserve makes hemodynamic and respiratory changes less tolerable
Older patients metabolize propofol faster
Older patients have larger airways and more dead space to clear
Age alone predicts difficult intubation and failed mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Age reduces cardiopulmonary reserve and increases drug sensitivity, so the same dose produces larger effects that are less well tolerated.

questions.stem: A patient takes 30 mg of oxycodone daily for back pain and is scheduled for a colonoscopy with sedation. Which planning approach is BEST?
options: Expect altered drug needs and titrate carefully
Avoid opioids to prevent synergy with propofol
Give naloxone before starting sedation
Dose exactly as for an opioid-naive adult
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid use produces tolerance and unpredictable responses. Expect different requirements, titrate carefully, and watch for exaggerated respiratory depression when drugs are combined.

questions.stem: A GI suite keeps its airway cart in the hallway "for emergencies." During a propofol case, the patient obstructs. What standard was violated?
options: Rescue devices must be immediately available before sedation starts
Rescue devices are needed for planned deep sedation
Rescue devices are needed for patients with known OSA
Rescue devices can be retrieved from the hallway cart once a problem actually occurs
questions.explanation: Airway rescue equipment must be immediately available before sedation begins, since depth can change without warning.

questions.stem: A patient's exam shows Mallampati II, good mouth opening, and full neck motion, but the thyromental distance is two fingerbreadths. Which finding MOST predicts a poor laryngoscopic view?
options: The short thyromental distance
The Mallampati II score on a seated exam
The good mouth opening
The full neck motion
questions.explanation: A short thyromental distance suggests a small mandibular space and an anterior larynx, predicting a poor view despite otherwise reassuring findings.

questions.stem: The Scenario 1 patient (Mallampati III, OSA, drapes over the face) tells you she is very anxious about being awake. What is the BEST approach?
options: Explain what to expect and give light anxiolysis carefully
Plan deep sedation to prevent any awareness
Cancel, since anxiety predicts poor cooperation under drapes
Use topical anesthesia alone with no sedation
questions.explanation: Anxiety is managed with expectation setting and careful anxiolysis. With Mallampati III, OSA, and limited airway access under drapes, deep sedation adds real risk.

questions.stem: A patient says, "I had trouble with a breathing tube last time." What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Obtain details and prior records to plan rescue
Reassure that sedation avoids airway problems
Proceed with deeper sedation to limit anxiety
Note it but proceed as usual
questions.explanation: Prior difficult intubation is a key history item. Details guide the rescue plan in case sedation becomes deeper than intended.

questions.stem: A CRNA is providing sedation for a colonoscopy. Which monitoring rule applies once an anesthesia provider is involved?
options: All standard ASA monitors must be applied
Pulse oximetry alone is sufficient
Monitoring depends on the gastroenterologist's request
ECG may be omitted if the patient is ASA I
questions.explanation: The lecture states that if an anesthesia provider is involved, all ASA monitors must be applied, regardless of the planned depth.

questions.stem: Per the monitoring table, how often must blood pressure be checked during MAC?
options: At least every 3–5 minutes
At least every 10 minutes
At least every 15 minutes
Continuously by arterial line
questions.explanation: The table lists BP at least every 3–5 minutes for MAC, every 5 minutes for moderate/deep procedural sedation, and at least every 3 minutes for TIVA/GA.

questions.stem: A patient for a long spine case is converted to TIVA after a failed sedation attempt. How often must BP now be measured at minimum?
options: At least every 3 minutes
At least every 5 minutes
Every 10 minutes
When the heart rate changes by more than 20%
questions.explanation: TIVA/GA calls for BP at least every 3 minutes, compared with at least every 5 minutes for MAC and moderate/deep sedation.

questions.stem: You provide care for two patients today: a healthy 30-year-old receiving moderate sedation from a sedation nurse for colonoscopy, and a 70-year-old with CAD receiving MAC from you for a TEE. A colleague says neither needs ECG "since both are just sedation." Which response is correct?
options: The MAC patient needs continuous ECG; the sedation patient's need depends on depth and risk
Neither needs ECG, since both are at sedation depths
Both need continuous ECG, since both received IV sedatives
The sedation patient needs ECG; the MAC patient does not, since an anesthetist is present
questions.explanation: During MAC the ECG is continuously displayed regardless of depth. During nurse-administered procedural sedation, ECG use is based on depth and patient risk, so a healthy patient at moderate depth may not need it.

questions.stem: You are moving between a procedural sedation case, a MAC case, and a TIVA case today. Which monitor is continuous in all three?
options: Heart rate and pulse oximetry
Core temperature
Invasive arterial pressure
Advanced hemodynamic monitoring
questions.explanation: Heart rate and pulse oximetry are continuous across procedural sedation, MAC, and TIVA/GA. Temperature and advanced hemodynamics depend on the setting and the patient.

questions.stem: A MAC case for a shoulder arthroscopy converts to TIVA after the block fails. How does temperature monitoring change?
options: It becomes continuous; under MAC it was used when indicated
It stays "as indicated," since the case began under MAC
It applies once the case runs over an hour
It requires a core probe in both settings
questions.explanation: Temperature is continuous during TIVA/GA and used when clinically indicated during procedural sedation and MAC.

questions.stem: A patient on 4 L nasal cannula during MAC has an SpO2 of 99% while her capnogram shows a respiratory rate of 5 and rising ETCO2. Why does capnography matter most here?
options: SpO2 lags behind hypoventilation on supplemental oxygen
Capnography directly measures sedation depth
Capnography can replace pulse oximetry
Pulse oximetry fails in most patients with dark skin
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen delays desaturation, so SpO2 can stay normal while ventilation fails. Capnography detects hypoventilation and apnea first.

questions.stem: A patient under propofol MAC has 4 L O2 by plain nasal cannula, SpO2 99%, and appears comfortable. The pump shows 150 mcg/kg/min. Twelve minutes later she is found with SpO2 82%. Which equipment change would have MOST likely detected the problem earliest?
options: A sampling nasal cannula connected to capnography
Increasing the oxygen flow to 6 L/min
A pulse oximeter with a variable-pitch tone
An NIBP cuff cycling every 3 minutes
questions.explanation: A sampling cannula detects hypoventilation and apnea immediately. More oxygen delays desaturation further, and SpO2 tones and BP cycling detect the problem late.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram A. A sedated patient's trace shows regular waveforms with a flat zero baseline and plateau values of 38–40. What is the BEST action?
options: Continue current care, since ventilation is adequate
Stimulate her and hold further sedative
Check for an exhausted CO2 absorber in the sampling line
Prepare for intubation
questions.explanation: Regular waveforms with a normal ETCO2 and zero baseline show adequate ventilation with no rebreathing.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram B. SpO2 is 97% on 3 L nasal cannula. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: Progressive hypoventilation masked by supplemental oxygen
Adequate ventilation because SpO2 is normal
Rising cardiac output after propofol
Sampling error from mouth breathing around the cannula
questions.explanation: Slowing rate and rising ETCO2 after propofol plus fentanyl indicate hypoventilation. Supplemental O2 keeps SpO2 normal, which is why SpO2 lags.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram B. During propofol sedation, the trace shows slow, widely spaced breaths with rising peak ETCO2. SpO2 is 97% on 4 L. What is the FIRST action?
options: Stimulate the patient, support ventilation, and hold further drug
Increase oxygen flow to 6 L/min and continue the infusion at the same rate
Give a propofol bolus to prevent movement
Continue observing, since SpO2 is still normal on oxygen
questions.explanation: Bradypnea with rising ETCO2 is hypoventilation. Stimulate, support the airway, and stop adding drug; normal SpO2 on oxygen is falsely reassuring.

questions.stem: Refer to Capnogram C. The waveform suddenly flattens while SpO2 reads 99%. What is the BEST first step?
options: Check the patient for apnea or obstruction immediately
Trust SpO2 and assume a sampling artifact for now
Reposition the sampling line and recheck the waveform
Deepen sedation to stop the gag and let the scope pass
questions.explanation: Loss of the capnogram is apnea, obstruction, or disconnection until proven otherwise. SpO2 lags, so assess the patient before attributing it to artifact.

questions.stem: Refer to the apnea timeline. Why does SpO2 stay near 99% for several minutes after breathing stops?
options: Supplemental oxygen raises oxygen reserve and delays desaturation
Pulse oximetry measures ventilation rather than oxygenation
Apnea increases cardiac output and oxygen delivery to tissues
Sedatives reduce oxygen consumption to zero
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation and supplemental O2 fill alveoli and blood with oxygen, so saturation falls only after reserve is used. ETCO2 changes immediately.

questions.stem: Refer to the apnea timeline. A patient on 6 L nasal cannula becomes apneic at 10:00. If only pulse oximetry were monitored, when would the problem first appear?
options: Several minutes after apnea begins
Within seconds of apnea
Before the apnea begins
Not at all, because supplemental oxygen keeps SpO2 normal
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen fills the FRC, so SpO2 stays normal for minutes after apnea. Capnography shows apnea immediately.

questions.stem: In Closed Claim Case 1, which monitors were in place when the patient was found apneic?
options: ECG, inspired oxygen, and ETCO2
Pulse oximetry alone
No monitors were applied
Blood pressure cuff and pulse oximetry
questions.explanation: Monitoring included ECG, inspired O2, and end-tidal CO2. The failure was not attending to the monitors, not a lack of them.

questions.stem: In Closed Claim Case 1, the patient was found apneic even though ECG, inspired oxygen, and ETCO2 were all in place. What does this teach?
options: Monitors help only when the provider is watching and acting on them
More monitors would have prevented the event on their own
ETCO2 does not detect apnea
The proceduralist should have been watching the monitors during the procedure
questions.explanation: Case 1 shows that applied monitors do not protect the patient without continuous attention and action.

questions.stem: In Closed Claim Case 2, a patient was sedated in holding and suffered an arrest during transport to the OR. What was the key failure?
options: No monitoring during transport after sedation
The wrong sedative was used
The patient was not intubated in holding
Too much oxygen was given during transport
questions.explanation: Once sedation is given, monitoring and airway readiness must continue during transport.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with severe AS is scheduled for TAVR under MAC, while a healthy 30-year-old is scheduled for MAC for a breast biopsy. What determines the use of advanced hemodynamic monitoring?
options: Patient condition and procedure factors
It is required for every MAC case
It is reserved for TIVA and GA cases
The proceduralist's preference alone
questions.explanation: Advanced hemodynamic monitoring during sedation and MAC depends on patient condition and procedure complexity. The TAVR patient likely needs it; the biopsy patient does not.

questions.stem: You are providing MAC for a hand surgery under a brachial plexus block. Which must be continuously monitored? (Select 3)
options: Heart rate
Pulse oximetry
ECG display
Core temperature
Invasive arterial pressure
Processed EEG
questions.explanation: During MAC, heart rate, SpO2, and ECG are continuous, along with ventilation. Temperature is used when indicated, and invasive or advanced monitoring depends on the patient.

questions.stem: A chart audit of a 3-hour MAC case shows SpO2 and ECG recorded continuously, BP every 5 minutes, and no capnography or temperature documented. The case was a 3-hour burn excision in a cool room. Which required elements are missing?
options: Ventilation monitoring and temperature monitoring
Processed EEG and invasive arterial pressure
Urine output and a second ECG lead
Nothing, since SpO2 covers ventilation
questions.explanation: MAC requires monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature when indicated. A long burn case in a cool room indicates temperature monitoring, and capnography was absent.

questions.stem: During sedation, ETCO2 climbs from 38 to 58 while SpO2 stays 98% on 4 L. Why should this concern you?
options: It shows hypoventilation before oxygenation fails
It shows the cannula is malfunctioning
It suggests the sampling cannula has shifted
It shows hyperventilation from anxiety under the drapes
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 means hypoventilation. On supplemental oxygen, SpO2 stays normal until reserves are exhausted.

questions.stem: A patient's nasal cannula capnogram reads 28 with a good waveform, but an ABG shows PaCO2 44. How should you use the cannula reading?
options: Trend it, since dilution makes the absolute value read low
Trust it, since cannula readings match PaCO2
Replace the cannula reading with intermittent ABGs
Replace it with pulse oximetry alone
questions.explanation: Nasal cannula sampling mixes exhaled gas with oxygen and room air, so values read low. The waveform and trend still reflect ventilation.

questions.stem: A patient's capnogram shows no waveform, but she is talking. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Mouth breathing or sampling line problem
Apnea with preserved speech
Complete airway obstruction with preserved speech
Malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: A talking patient is breathing. A lost waveform is then likely technical or due to mouth breathing, but you still verify at the bedside.

questions.stem: A proceduralist says pulse oximetry is enough because "if she stops breathing, the sat will drop." Why is this wrong during moderate sedation?
options: SpO2 detects hypoxemia late and does not measure ventilation
SpO2 overestimates oxygenation during sedation
SpO2 overestimates the severity of hypoventilation
SpO2 is unreliable in patients with light skin under the procedure lights
questions.explanation: SpO2 measures oxygenation and lags, especially on oxygen. Capnography detects hypoventilation and apnea directly.

questions.stem: A department reviews 40 sedation adverse events: 22 involved hypoventilation or obstruction, 6 aspiration, 5 hypotension, 4 medication errors, and 3 allergic reactions. Which conclusion is BEST supported?
options: Respiratory events are the dominant source and should drive the safety plan
Cardiovascular events are the dominant source
Medication errors are the dominant source
The events are evenly distributed, so no single focus is needed
questions.explanation: Hypoventilation, obstruction, and aspiration account for 28 of 40 events, consistent with respiratory events being a major source of adverse sedation outcomes.

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient's SpO2 falls from 98% to 91%. ETCO2 waveform is absent. What does this sequence indicate?
options: Ventilation failure has been ongoing and is now causing hypoxemia
A new and brief event that just began
Pulse oximeter error from peripheral vasoconstriction in the finger
Improved ventilation after a painful stimulus
questions.explanation: By the time SpO2 falls on supplemental O2, apnea or obstruction has usually been present for some time. Treat urgently.

questions.stem: During MAC for a bronchoscopy, the patient develops laryngospasm. Which monitor shows the problem FIRST?
options: Capnography, with a flat or absent waveform
Pulse oximetry, with an immediate drop
ECG, with ST changes
NIBP, with a BP rise
questions.explanation: Capnography loses its waveform as soon as airflow stops; SpO2 lags and ECG and BP changes come later.

questions.stem: A proceduralist asks you to remove the capnography cannula because it irritates the patient's nose during moderate sedation. What is the BEST response?
options: Keep capnography, since ETCO2 monitoring is required during sedation
Remove it if SpO2 stays above 95% on supplemental oxygen
Remove it and watch the chest rise instead, since SpO2 is normal on oxygen
Switch to a non-rebreather without CO2 sampling
questions.explanation: Capnography is required during moderate and deep sedation. Reposition or change the cannula, but keep monitoring ventilation.

questions.stem: A nurse-monitored sedation protocol for deep sedation lists BP checks every 15 minutes "if vitals are stable." What is the correct minimum frequency?
options: At least every 5 minutes during moderate or deep sedation
Every 15 minutes, since the vitals are stable
Continuous arterial monitoring for all deep sedation
At the start and end of the procedure
questions.explanation: BP should be measured at least every 5 minutes during moderate and deep procedural sedation. Stable vitals do not lengthen the interval.

questions.stem: Two sedated patients each have an ETCO2 of 58. Patient A breathes 6 times per minute with large breaths. Patient B breathes 30 times per minute with tiny breaths. What do both readings MAINLY indicate?
options: Inadequate alveolar ventilation in both
Adequate ventilation in A, inadequate in B
Low cardiac output in both
Hypoxemia in both
questions.explanation: ETCO2 in a spontaneously breathing patient reflects alveolar ventilation. Bradypnea and rapid shallow breathing can both leave alveolar ventilation inadequate.

questions.stem: Refer to the apnea timeline. A patient on 6 L nasal cannula stops breathing at minute 2. Which sequence of monitor changes is MOST likely?
options: ETCO2 drops at once; SpO2 stays normal for minutes
SpO2 drops first; ETCO2 then confirms the apnea
Both monitors change at the same moment
ETCO2 changes after desaturation begins
questions.explanation: The capnogram flattens at the onset of apnea while SpO2 holds for minutes on supplemental oxygen. That lag is why capnography is central during sedation.

questions.stem: Which of the following help detect hypoventilation during sedation? (Select 2)
options: Capnography waveform
Respiratory rate and depth
Pulse oximetry trend on supplemental oxygen
Blood pressure trend
Temperature trend
ECG heart rate
questions.explanation: Capnography and respiratory rate and depth assess ventilation directly. SpO2 lags on supplemental oxygen, and BP, temperature, and HR do not measure breathing.

questions.stem: A patient under MAC has ETCO2 rising from 38 to 55 over 10 minutes with slowing respirations. SpO2 is 98%. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Cumulative respiratory depression from drug synergy
Rising CO2 production from hyperthermia under drapes
Increased cardiac output from pain and anxiety
Rebreathing from exhausted CO2 absorbent in the circuit
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 with slow breathing after sedatives and opioids indicates cumulative respiratory depression. The synergy is emphasized in the lecture.

questions.stem: A MAC case for a breast lumpectomy is converted to TIVA with an LMA. Which monitoring change is required?
options: Temperature monitoring becomes continuous
Heart rate monitoring becomes intermittent
ECG changes from displayed to continuously recorded
ECG changes to intermittent display
questions.explanation: Moving to TIVA/GA makes temperature monitoring continuous. Heart rate, SpO2, and ECG stay continuous.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with CAD is receiving deep sedation for a cardioversion. Which statement about ECG monitoring is correct?
options: ECG is routinely used for deeper sedation
ECG is unnecessary if SpO2 is continuous
ECG is used during MAC but is optional in deep sedation
ECG is needed when temperature is monitored
questions.explanation: For procedural sedation, ECG use is based on depth and risk and is routinely used for deeper sedation. This patient needs it for both reasons.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD is receiving MAC and has a baseline ETCO2 of 50. What matters MOST when interpreting her capnography?
options: Changes from her baseline trend
The absolute value compared with 40
The SpO2 value in isolation
Whether she is on room air
questions.explanation: Some patients have chronically elevated CO2. The trend and waveform are more useful than a single absolute number.

questions.stem: A patient on 4 L oxygen under sedation has SpO2 99%. Which statements about pulse oximetry are correct? (Select 3)
options: It is continuously monitored during sedation, MAC, and TIVA/GA
It lags behind hypoventilation when oxygen is given
It reflects oxygenation, not ventilation
It detects apnea within seconds
It replaces capnography for moderate sedation
It is needed during deep sedation but not moderate
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is continuous in every setting and reflects oxygenation. On oxygen it lags hypoventilation, so it cannot replace capnography.

questions.stem: During MAC, why must the provider keep eyes on both patient and monitors while the proceduralist talks?
options: Distraction led to unrecognized apnea in a closed claim
Talking disturbs the capnography sampling
The proceduralist controls sedation depth
Talking increases the risk of laryngospasm in the patient
questions.explanation: Case 1 showed that conversation with the gastroenterologist led to loss of situational awareness and unrecognized apnea.

questions.stem: During TIVA for a craniotomy, propofol boluses are given every few minutes. The NIBP is set to cycle every 5 minutes, and a BP of 72/40 goes unnoticed for 4 minutes. What monitoring standard was missed?
options: BP at least every 3 minutes under TIVA/GA
BP at least every 5 minutes under TIVA/GA
BP every 10 minutes when vitals are stable
Continuous arterial pressure for all TIVA cases
questions.explanation: TIVA/GA requires BP at least every 3 minutes; the 5-minute interval applies to moderate and deep procedural sedation.

questions.stem: During MAC for a TEE, a patient's ECG leads are removed for probe positioning and not replaced for 15 minutes. SpO2 is 98% and NIBP is cycling. A brief run of VT occurs during this time but is not seen. What standard was violated?
options: Continuous ECG display throughout MAC
ECG display at induction and emergence
ECG display for patients with known arrhythmias
ECG display when SpO2 falls below 92%
questions.explanation: MAC requires the ECG to be continuously displayed for the entire case. Pulse oximetry and NIBP cannot detect arrhythmias like VT.

questions.stem: After a sedation bolus, which is the EARLIEST sign of respiratory depression on standard monitors?
options: Change in capnogram rate and waveform
SpO2 falling below 90% on the monitor
Heart rate slowing on the ECG tracing
Blood pressure rising on the NIBP cycle
questions.explanation: Capnography reflects each breath, so changes in rate and pattern appear first. SpO2, HR, and BP change later.

questions.stem: Three MAC cases are scheduled: a 15-minute cataract, a 20-minute colonoscopy, and a 4-hour burn dressing change with large exposed areas. In which case is temperature monitoring clearly indicated?
options: The 4-hour burn dressing change
The 15-minute cataract surgery
The 20-minute colonoscopy
All three, since temperature is continuous for MAC
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring during MAC is required when clinically indicated, such as long cases with large exposed surface areas. It is continuous under TIVA/GA.

questions.stem: A propofol and remifentanil sedation drifts too deep during the quiet middle of a case, then too light at the painful end. Which factors should guide titration? (Select 4)
options: Drug kinetics
Effect-site delay
Changing procedural stimulus
Drug interactions
The proceduralist's preferred depth
The patient's stated fear of needles
questions.explanation: Titration should account for kinetics, effect-site delay, drug interactions, and changing stimulus. Matching depth to the stimulus prevents both overshoot and undershoot.

questions.stem: You give a propofol bolus, see little effect after 30 seconds, and give another. A minute later, the patient is apneic. Why?
options: Peak effect lags injection, so the boluses stacked
Propofol's rapid redistribution ended the first dose early
The second bolus was absorbed faster
Propofol's effect builds with each heartbeat
questions.explanation: Effect-site delay means the first bolus had not peaked when the second was given, so their effects combined.

questions.stem: A patient at moderate sedation shows ETCO2 of 45 with regular waveforms and RR 12. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: Adequate ventilation with a slightly elevated but stable value
Severe hypoventilation needing immediate reversal agents given
Apnea that needs airway rescue
Hyperventilation from pain
questions.explanation: A regular waveform and normal rate with a stable ETCO2 in the mid 40s is acceptable. The trend matters more than one mildly elevated value.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST summarizes monitoring requirements for any case involving an anesthesia provider?
options: Standard ASA monitors are applied regardless of depth
Monitoring intensity depends on ASA class
Depth-specific monitors are what is required
Monitors can be removed once the patient is stable
questions.explanation: The lecture states that if an anesthesia provider is involved, all ASA monitors must be applied.

questions.stem: During sedation, the capnogram disappears every time the patient opens her mouth wide to breathe. SpO2 and chest movement are normal. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: The nasal sampling line misses gas exhaled through the mouth
She has become apneic from oversedation with propofol
She is in bronchospasm
The CO2 absorbent in the sampling module is exhausted
questions.explanation: Nasal sampling captures exhaled gas from the nose, so mouth breathing can make the waveform disappear despite normal ventilation.

questions.stem: During deep sedation for a hip reduction, BP readings are 132/80 at 10:00, then 128/78 at 10:15, then 70/40 at 10:30. Which statement about this monitoring is correct?
options: The interval was too long; BP should be checked at least every 5 minutes
The interval was appropriate because the first readings were stable
The interval was appropriate for deep sedation
The interval was acceptable because the first readings were stable
questions.explanation: Moderate and deep procedural sedation requires BP at least every 5 minutes; 15-minute intervals allowed hypotension to go unnoticed.

questions.stem: In both closed claims cases, monitors were available but the patient still suffered harm. What common gap explains both?
options: A lapse in watching or applying monitors after sedation
Defective monitoring equipment
Absence of capnography in both cases
The monitors failed to alarm in both cases
questions.explanation: Both cases show that harm follows lapses in attention or monitoring after sedation, not equipment failure.

questions.stem: A patient's ETCO2 waveform becomes smaller and irregular, and you hear snoring. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: Partial upper airway obstruction
Complete laryngospasm with no air movement
Esophageal intubation
Hyperventilation from pain
questions.explanation: Snoring with small, irregular waveforms suggests partial obstruction. Jaw thrust or repositioning is often the fix.

questions.stem: You are setting up a remote endoscopy room for MAC. What must be immediately available? (Select 4)
options: Suction
Emergency drugs
Advanced airway equipment
Oxygen and a means of positive-pressure ventilation
A running anesthesia machine vaporizer
A neuromonitoring technician
questions.explanation: The MAC environment requires oxygen, suction, ventilation equipment, emergency drugs, capnography, and advanced airway equipment.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old receives only oral midazolam (minimal sedation) for a dental procedure, with an anesthesia provider present. What monitoring applies?
